hookLine: In 2003, in a Hampshire village shop, sub-postmistress Jo Hamilton watched her computer invent a debt in front of her.

captions.text: In 2003, in a Hampshire village shop,

sub-postmistress Jo Hamilton watched her computer
invent a debt in front of her.

The screen said two thousand pounds was missing
from her post-office till —
money she had never seen.

She phoned the helpline and followed
its instructions —

and while she was on the line, the missing two
thousand became four.
She remortgaged her house to pay it.

Her employer prosecuted her anyway — for theft,
in front of her whole village.

But the money never existed. The computer
was lying.

The people who owned it knew — and proving
that would take twenty-one years,
and an Act of Parliament like no other.

What happened in that village shop happened,
in some form,

to roughly a thousand people — prosecuted
on the word of one machine,
most by their own employer, across sixteen years,

while warning after warning was put in writing
and filed away. England, 1999.
It begins with an upgrade.

A sub-postmaster is not quite a shopkeeper
and not quite a civil servant.

In Britain, the post office counter usually lives
inside somebody's shop —
the newsagent, the grocer —

and the person behind it is a private citizen
who has bought the right

to serve their village on behalf
of a centuries-old national institution.

They hand out pensions on Thursdays. They take
in Christmas savings.

They know which customer needs the forms read
aloud to them.
In thousands of villages,

the sub-postmaster was the closest thing
the community had to a bank, a notary,
and a friend with an official stamp.

The red sign over the door meant the same thing
on every high street in the country:

the state, in walking distance, with a familiar
face behind the counter.

People queued at nine for their pensions
and stayed to talk.

The sub-postmaster cashed their cheques, weighed
their parcels,

kept their confidences. It was a good life —
modest, respected, permanent.
The people in this story did not drift into it.

They bought their way in, with their savings
and their houses,

because running a village post office
was the safest thing a careful family

could do with its money. People paid
for that privilege.
In May 1998,
a man named Alan Bates

and his partner Suzanne Sercombe put sixty-five
thousand pounds of their own money

into a small post office in Craig-y-Don,
on the North Wales coast.

He was a careful man — the kind who kept receipts,
filed paperwork,

backed up his backups. That detail will matter
more than anything else in this film.

In 1999, the Post Office began rolling out a new
computer system
to every branch counter in the country.

It was called Horizon, built by the British firm
ICL under its Japanese owner,

Fujitsu, and it was described at the time
as the biggest non-military IT contract

in Europe. The terminals arrived the way
the future usually does —
as an instruction.

The paper ledgers that sub-postmasters
had balanced by hand were carried out,

and from that day the branch's truth was whatever
the screen said it was.
Most branches got on with it.

The machine was modern, the institution
was centuries old,

and nobody buys a village post office expecting
to need a lawyer.
By late 2001, Horizon was everywhere.
And almost at once, in shop after shop,

the same strange scene began to play
out at closing time.

A sub-postmistress cashes up. She counts the till
twice.

The cash in her hand and the number on the screen
do not agree —

the screen says money is missing. Not a rounding
error: hundreds of pounds.

Sometimes thousands, appearing overnight,
between locking the door and unlocking it.

In Craig-y-Don, Horizon arrived in October 2000;
by December,

Alan Bates was staring at an unexplained hole
of around six thousand pounds.
He did what everyone did. He rang the helpline.

The search that came first played out behind
thousands of those counters.
You count the till again. You count the safe.

You go back through the week's receipts line
by line, hunting for your own mistake —

because it must be your mistake; the alternative
is unthinkable.

Husbands and wives sat up past midnight
with shoeboxes of paper,

checking each other's arithmetic against a machine
that would not show its own.

The screen did not argue. It simply repeated
the number.

The helpline had an answer, and the answer never
changed.

No one else is having this problem. You
are the only one.

The inquiry that finally examined this scandal
heard that sentence described

by sub-postmaster after sub-postmaster — the same
reassurance,

delivered up and down the country, to hundreds
of people at once,

each of them alone in a dark shop with a number
that could not be true.

It was not a small lie. It was the load-bearing
lie.

If you are the only one, the machine is fine —
and the problem is you.

And here the trap closed, because of a clause most
of them had never dwelt on.
Under their contracts,

sub-postmasters were personally liable for losses
shown in their accounts.

The court that later tore this system apart put it
simply:

Horizon offered no way for a sub-postmaster
to dispute Horizon's own figures.

The screen said the money was gone; the contract
said the shortfall was yours;

and the institution treated an illusion as a debt.
So they paid. From savings.
From remortgages. From their parents.

And some of them — exhausted, frightened, assured
they were alone —

pressed the button that said the accounts balanced
when they did not,
just to keep trading until someone sorted it out.
British law has a name for pressing that button.

It is called false accounting, and it carries
a criminal record.
Alan Bates refused to press it.
He refused to sign for phantom losses at all,

and he sent the Post Office letter after letter
saying precisely why.

In November 2003, the Post Office terminated
his contract without giving a reason —

its own files, disclosed years later, called him
unmanageable.

He lost the shop and the sixty-five thousand
pounds.

What the Post Office did not know was that it
had just fired the one man in Britain

who would never, ever let it go. Then the letters
changed.

Because the Post Office was not only
these people's employer,

their landlord of last resort, and the author
of their contracts.

In England and Wales, any company may bring
a private prosecution —
and the Post Office did, on an industrial scale.

When a shortfall appeared, the Post Office
investigated the crime,

and the Post Office decided the charge,
and the Post Office prosecuted the case.
Victim, detective, and prosecutor, in one body.

The police were not called, because the police
were not needed.
Between 1999 and 2015,

roughly seven hundred sub-postmasters
were prosecuted by the Post Office itself —

on average, about one a week, for a decade
and a half.

And keep one number running from here to the end
of this film:

the number of Post Office or Fujitsu employees
convicted of anything
for what you are about to watch. It never changes.

The method was consistent enough that a court
would later describe it
in cold detail.

Investigators would arrive, suspend
the sub-postmaster on the spot,

and interview them under caution — the Post
Office's own staff,
playing detective in the shop the suspect owned.

The charge sheet carried two counts: theft,
and false accounting.

Theft was the hammer — it meant prison, headlines,
ruin.

And then, quietly, an offer: plead guilty to false
accounting,

pay back the shortfall, and the theft charge goes
away.

Jo Hamilton learned how the lever worked
when the Post Office said her little shop

in South Warnborough was thirty-six thousand
pounds down.

Its own investigators had reported, in writing,
that there was no evidence of theft.

She was charged with theft anyway — and offered
the trade:

plead guilty to fourteen counts of false
accounting, repay thirty-six thousand,

six hundred and forty-four pounds, and the theft
count disappears.
She took it, the way almost everyone took it,

because the alternative was a trial she
could not afford to lose,
in front of people she had served for years.

A criminal record, for the crime of believing
her employer's computer.

The court's file preserves the Post Office's
condition in its own words:
a plea "on the basis that the loss was due

to the computer not working properly
will not be accepted.
In the case of Noel Thomas —

a Welsh postman of forty-two years' service
who ran the counter at Gaerwen,
on Anglesey — the record is even blunter:

his guilty plea would be accepted only
on the basis that he accepted
that Horizon was working perfectly.

You could have your freedom, if you agreed
the machine was innocent.

Thomas went to prison for a forty-eight-thousand-pound
shortfall that never existed.
He turned sixty inside.
Around the same era,

guidance issued to Post Office investigators
was sorting the people they interviewed
into racial categories —

a document that would not surface for another
fifteen years.
Not everyone could be pushed to a plea.

Lee Castleton ran the post office in Bridlington,
on the Yorkshire coast.

From January 2004 his screen conjured shortfall
after shortfall —

around twenty-five thousand pounds — and he
refused to accept the debt was real,
because he had counted his own till.

So the Post Office took him to the High Court,
in a civil suit,

where there is no jury and the loser pays
the winner's lawyers.

Castleton had no money for barristers; he
represented himself,

a shopkeeper alone against an institution. He
lost.

And with the verdict came the bill for the Post
Office's costs:
three hundred and twenty-one thousand pounds.

He was bankrupted — over a phantom debt
one-thirteenth that size.

His wife began having seizures brought
on by stress.

His children were bullied at school. The family
lost everything.

The Post Office never collected most of the money.
Collection was not the point.

The point was what happened to the next
sub-postmaster who thought about fighting.

And then there is Seema Misra. She ran the post
office at West Byfleet, in Surrey.

In January 2008 an audit found her branch
seventy-nine thousand pounds short
on Horizon's ledger.
She had put in her own money;
she had told the helpline again and again

that the system was generating losses she
could not explain.

She was charged with theft — the sum
on the indictment, seventy-four thousand,
six hundred and nine pounds and eighty-four pence,

calculated to the penny by a machine
that could not do arithmetic.
At Guildford Crown Court in October 2010,

the Post Office's expert witness assured the jury
the system was reliable.
She was convicted.

On the eleventh of November 2010 — her son's tenth
birthday —

Seema Misra was sent to prison for fifteen months.
She was eight weeks pregnant.
She served her time at Bronzefield,

and when her second son was born the following
summer,
she was wearing an electronic tag.

A pregnant woman went to prison on the word
of a computer.

That sentence should be impossible to write
about modern Britain.

Now here is the one that is worse: eleven weeks
before her jury came back,

the Post Office had already put in writing what
would happen

if anyone looked too closely at the machine.
August 2010.

An internal report lands on senior desks
at the Post Office,

written by the head of product and branch
accounting.

Its subject: how to respond to challenges
to Horizon's integrity.

Its logic, in the Post Office's own preserved
words, is this:

any independent investigation of the system
would have to be disclosed in court —

and "any perception that POL doubts its own
systems would mean

that all criminal prosecutions
would have to be stayed.

It would also beg a question for the Court
of Appeal over past prosecutions

and imprisonments." There it is, in one paragraph,
in 2010.

Check the machine honestly, and every prosecution
stops.

Check the machine honestly, and the ones already
in prison get to appeal.

The institution had written down the price
of the truth — and decided,
prosecution by prosecution, not to pay it.

Seema Misra was convicted eleven weeks
after that report.
The expert who vouched for Horizon

at her trial was a Fujitsu engineer named Gareth
Jenkins,

whose standard assurance was that the system
"will accurately record all data

that is submitted to it and correctly account
for it.

The Court of Appeal would later record he
had known

of live Horizon bugs since September of that same
year —
and said nothing about them in his evidence.

Because the bugs were real, and inside Fujitsu
they had names.

The Callendar Square bug, known
about since the mid-2000s,
which duplicated transactions.
The receipts-and-payments mismatch bug of 2010 —

an internal note records discrepancies that vanish
from the counter screen

"but will still show within the back end branch
account," quietly corrupting

the books of some forty branches. Their existence
was not folklore.
It was ticketed, logged,

and discussed on the vendor's side of a wall
the sub-postmasters could not see.

And on the far side of that wall sat something
even the bugs could not match

for secrecy: a support centre in Bracknell where
Fujitsu engineers could reach

into a branch's live accounts and change
the numbers —

without the sub-postmaster ever knowing anyone
had been there.

For years, the Post Office's public position
was that this was flatly impossible.

In 2012, under pressure from MPs led by James
Arbuthnot,

the Post Office appointed independent
investigators —
a small forensic accountancy firm, Second Sight —
and for a moment it looked like daylight.
Their first report, in July 2013,
confirmed two live defects and a support system
that failed the very people it existed to help.

That same month, the Post Office's own barrister,
Simon Clarke,
delivered a devastating legal advice:

the expert evidence underpinning years
of prosecutions was unreliable,
because the expert had known about the bugs.
Weeks later, Clarke recorded something darker.

The Post Office had set up weekly calls to track
Horizon's defects —

and then someone gave an instruction
about the minutes of those calls.

The advice preserves it in one sentence:
the emails and minutes "should be,

and have been, destroyed: the word 'shredded'
was conveyed to me.

The thinking, as recorded, was simpler still:
if it's not minuted,
it's not disclosable.

That summer — the summer its own lawyer used
the word shredded —

the Post Office was wearing down a man named
Martin Griffiths.

He had run the post office on Hope Farm Road
in Ellesmere Port since 1995.

From 2009, the shortfalls came, and the helpline
told him what it told everyone —

his family say he was made to feel he was the only
one,

while the same complaint poured in from across
the country.

He repaid and repaid; his elderly parents put
in their life savings,
about sixty-two thousand pounds.
In May 2013 his branch was robbed,

and the Post Office's investigator held him partly
responsible for the stolen money.
In July 2013, it gave him notice of termination.
On the twenty-third of September 2013,

Martin Griffiths deliberately walked in front
of a moving bus.

He died in hospital eighteen days later. He
was fifty-nine.

The Post Office later reached a confidential
settlement with his family.

The public inquiry would eventually be told
of at least thirteen people

who took their own lives in connection
with this scandal,

and of at least fifty-nine more who contemplated
it.

Watch what the institution did next, because it
is the tell.

The prosecutions quietly stopped — from forty-two
in a single year to two,

then zero — with no announcement, no review
of the convictions already won,
no letter to the people already ruined.

In March 2015, the Post Office sacked Second Sight
and,

as Arbuthnot told the House of Commons that week,
told it to destroy all its papers.
In January 2015,

preparing to face a committee of MPs
on the question of remote access,

chief executive Paula Vennells wrote in an email
disclosed years later

to the public inquiry: "I need to say no it
is not possible.

A High Court judgment would later quote what
the chief executive's office was asking

behind closed doors that January: "What
is the true answer?
I hope it is that we know this is not possible.

Its formal answer to Parliament that same winter
was absolute:

there is "no functionality in Horizon for either
a branch,
Post Office or Fujitsu to edit,

manipulate or remove transaction data once it
has been recorded
in a branch's accounts.

And when the BBC's Panorama put the question
directly that summer,

with a former Fujitsu engineer named Richard Roll
saying on camera

that engineers could and did reach into branch
accounts,
the Post Office denied it again.

Every part of that sentence would die
in a courtroom.

It just needed someone with twenty years
of patience to carry it there.
The army had been forming since 2009.

In May of that year, a trade magazine — Computer
Weekly —

had published the first story anyone dared
to print,

by a young reporter named Rebecca Thomson: seven
sub-postmasters,

seven impossible shortfalls, one system. Alan
Bates was one of the seven.

That November, he hired a village hall in Fenny
Compton, Warwickshire —

picked more or less at random, because it sat
in the middle of England —

and invited whoever else was out there. A couple
of dozen strangers walked in.
They had never met.

Each of them had been told, for years, that they
were the only one.

They looked around a room full of only-ones,
and they gave themselves a name:
the Justice for Subpostmasters Alliance.

The press lane stayed narrow, but it never quite
closed.

In November 2010 a radio reporter named Nick
Wallis took a call

from a man whose pregnant wife had just been sent
to prison over a till

that would not balance — Seema Misra's husband,
Davinder.

Wallis spent the next decade on the story
when almost nobody else would touch it,

on regional television, then in Private Eye,
eventually in a book.

The facts were available for years to anyone
who looked. Almost nobody looked.
What followed was not a montage;

it was a grind that consumed the better part
of two decades.

Bates ran the campaign the way he had run
his branch — from a kitchen table,

on a laptop, with files. He wrote to ministers
and was patted on the head.

He gathered members in the dozens, then
the hundreds.

And in 2017, five hundred and fifty-five
sub-postmasters,

bankrolled by litigation funders because none
of them had money left,

sued the Post Office in the High Court
under a single group action.

The lead name on the claim, alphabetically
and in every other sense:

Bates versus Post Office. The institution fought
like an institution.
It ran up costs designed to outlast the funders.

In March 2019, when the first judgment savaged
its sub-postmaster contracts,

it did something almost unheard of: mid-trial, it
applied to remove the judge,
Mr Justice Fraser, from the case.

The application failed within weeks,
and the appeal court refused to touch it.
And in December 2019,

Fraser handed down the judgment the Post Office
had spent twenty years making sure
no one would ever write.

The shoeboxes of receipts
and the backed-up backups had finally met a judge

who read every page. Legacy Horizon, he found,
was "not remotely robust.

The Post Office's approach to the mounting
evidence, he wrote,

"demonstrates a simple institutional obstinacy
or refusal

to consider any possible alternatives
to their view of Horizon" —

its insistence on the system's integrity amounted
to "the 21st century equivalent
of maintaining that the earth is flat.

And the denials about Bracknell collapsed
entirely.

Remote access to branch accounts, the court found,
"does exist;

such remote access is possible by employees within
Fujitsu;

it does exist specifically by design; and it
has been used in the past.

The Post Office's years of public assurances were,
in the judge's words,
"specifically wrong in fact.

Before Christmas, Fraser referred his concerns
about the evidence

of Fujitsu's witnesses to the Director of Public
Prosecutions. The 555 had won.
Now look at what winning bought them.

The Post Office had in fact already seen enough:
days before the judgment came down,

it settled — fifty-seven point seven five million
pounds.
And after the litigation funders and the lawyers
who had made the case possible took their share,

the sub-postmasters were left with roughly twelve
million between them.

About twenty thousand pounds each, for ruined
businesses, bankruptcies, and prison.

Alan Bates had beaten the Post Office in open
court
and could not even cover his members' losses.

But the judgment was never really about the money.
It was a key.

Criminal convictions built on a machine now
judicially certified
as unreliable could finally be appealed —

and the Criminal Cases Review Commission began
referring them in batches.

In December 2020, the first six convictions fell
at Southwark Crown Court.

And on the twenty-third of April 2021,
at the Royal Courts of Justice,

the Court of Appeal ruled on thirty-nine more —
and did not merely quash them.

It found the Post Office had known. "POL knew
that there were problems with Horizon.

POL knew that SPMs around the country
had complained of inexplicable discrepancies…

In short, POL knew that there were serious issues
about the reliability of Horizon.
It had, the court said,

"effectively steamrolled over any SPM who sought
to challenge its accuracy" —

and its failures were "so egregious as to make
the prosecution of any

of the 'Horizon cases' an affront
to the conscience of the court.
On the pavement outside stood Jo Hamilton,

eighteen years after a helpline talked her debt
from two thousand pounds to four —
no longer, in the eyes of the law, a thief.

Cameras caught her half-laughing, half-crying,
holding the paperwork.
Thirty-nine names cleared.

Then more, in batches through 2022 and 2023 —
about a hundred in all.

Which left roughly nine hundred convictions still
standing, held by people now old,

or ill, or dead, many of whom would not go near
a courtroom again for anything.

At the pace the system was managing, the last
of them would die convicted.

That is where this story stood on New Year's Eve,
2023.

What broke the logjam was not a judgment,
and not a report.
It was a television schedule.
On the first of January 2024,

ITV began a four-night drama called Mr Bates vs
the Post Office —

actors playing Bates, Hamilton, Misra,
the helpline calls, the shredded minutes,
the whole quarter-century. Nothing in it was new.

Every fact had been in the public record
for years,

in judgments almost nobody outside the campaign
had read.

But close to ten million people watched it
in a week —
thirteen and a half million by spring —

and Britain went from not knowing the story
to being unable
to think about anything else.
Within days, more

than 1.2 million people signed a petition
demanding Paula Vennells lose her CBE —

the honour she had been given in 2019,
for services to the Post Office.

On the ninth of January she announced: "I return
my CBE with immediate effect.
On the tenth,

the Prime Minister stood up in Parliament
and promised something without precedent.
The running number —

employees of the Post Office or Fujitsu convicted
for any of this —
stood at zero on the night the drama aired.

It is worth watching closely through the reckoning
that follows.
On the twenty-fourth of May 2024,

the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act
received royal assent.

Its first sentence does something no British law
had ever done at this scale:

"Every conviction to which this Act applies
is quashed on the coming into force
of this Act. Not reviewed. Not referred.

Quashed — hundreds of convictions, at the stroke
of the King's pen,

most of them without any court ever looking
at the individual case again.
In England and Wales alone,

six hundred and nineteen people have so far
been identified as cleared by the Act.
Parliament had already, back in January,
rushed through a first Act to get money moving;

the cleared were offered six hundred thousand
pounds each, full and final —

or a longer, harder road if they believed
their losses were bigger.

The country's most senior former judges rose
in the House of Lords to object,

and their objection measures the failure:
Parliament does not quash convictions,

said the former Lord Chief Justice —
that is a matter for the courts. He was right.
That is exactly how bad it had become:

the miscarriage was too big for the courts
that caused it,

and the constitution had to be bent to clear
the innocent in bulk.
The calendar of that week is its own verdict.

On the very Friday the Act received the King's
assent, across London,

Paula Vennells was completing three days
of evidence to the public inquiry —

under a barrister's questions about the email
that said I need to say no,

about what she had been told, and when. She wept
repeatedly.
"I was too trusting," she told the inquiry.

Three months earlier, the King had formally erased
her honour;

the notice in the official Gazette records
that her CBE was "cancelled and annulled.
It remains, to date,

one of the very few individual consequences anyone
connected
to this scandal has faced.

In July 2025, the inquiry's chairman, Sir Wyn
Williams,

published the first volume of his final report —
the human accounting.

Roughly one thousand people prosecuted
and convicted on Horizon evidence.

About ten thousand people now eligible
for redress.

At least thirteen suicides linked to the scandal,
a number he said may be higher.

His word for the impact was "disastrous,"
and his finding was that these people

were victims of "wholly unacceptable behaviour" —
by individuals,

and by the Post Office and Fujitsu
"as institutions.
He attached nineteen recommendations,
and a deadline for the institutions to answer him.
By the summer of 2026,

the government's ledger showed about one point six
billion pounds paid out to more

than twelve thousand nine hundred claimants — real
money at last,
though Sir Alan Bates, knighted in 2024,

was by then writing that the schemes
had been turned into "quasi-kangaroo courts" —
his own offer less than half of what he had lost.

Fujitsu told Parliament in January 2024 it
had a "moral obligation" to contribute.

As of the middle of 2026, it had contributed
nothing —

and its engineers still run Horizon, on a contract
extended to 2027,

because the machine at the centre of all
of this is still, today,

on the counters of Britain's post offices.
So finish the count.

Roughly one thousand people convicted on the word
of a broken machine.

About seven hundred of them prosecuted
by their own employer — one a week,
for fifteen years.

By the BBC's count, two hundred and thirty-six
of them went to prison.

At least thirteen people are dead by their own
hand.

And the number of human beings convicted of any
crime for doing this to them —
after the shredded minutes, the buried advice,

the denials a High Court judge called specifically
wrong in fact — is still zero.
A police investigation with more

than a hundred officers has fifty-three people
under examination;

it does not expect to put files before prosecutors
until late 2027.

The inquiry volumes that will name the culpable
are, as of this summer,

still unpublished. The detective leading
the criminal case said it plainly

this spring: many victims are old now, some
are already gone —

"we do not have the luxury of time." Somewhere
in England tomorrow morning,
a shutter will go up over a post-office counter,
and the screen behind it will still say Horizon.

The system was told the truth about itself
in 2010, in writing,
and calculated that the truth was unaffordable.

It spent the next decade buying time with other
people's lives — and the bill,

so far, has been paid by everyone except
the people who wrote it.
One more line of the ledger deserves its place.

For years, a helpline told frightened people, one
call at a time,

that they were the only one. There turned
out to be ten thousand of them.

The sentence was a lie the first time it
was spoken and a lie every time after —

and the cure for it, in the end, was not a court,
and not a law.
It was a village hall in the middle of England,

and a handful of ruined shopkeepers discovering
that the only-ones were an army.

If you think a machine's word should never
outweigh a human being's —

and that someone, eventually, must answer
for the ones it buried — hit like,

so the next story like this gets told before it
takes twenty years.
